title: Full-Bandwidth Transformer: Feed the Hidden State Back
hook: Between decoding steps a transformer throws away everything except the sampled token. Widening that channel with the top-layer hidden state buys roughly 1.5x the training tokens' worth of quality.
key_points: Standard autoregressive decoding passes only the sampled token to the next step; the top-layer hidden state is discarded.
The full-bandwidth transformer fuses that previous hidden state with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and feeds it back as the next input.
This lets non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a fresh depth budget, while keeping the standard architecture, KV cache, and language-modeling objective.
Training uses a scheduled multi-pass objective — latent feedback is introduced late in pretraining, with a fraction of deeper passes for stability — to preserve parallel teacher forcing.
At 1B parameters and 400B tokens, the authors report gains in validation loss, 5-shot evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance.
The reported effect is roughly matching a standard transformer trained on ~1.5x more tokens, at negligible per-token decoding overhead — with shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.
content_html: An autoregressive transformer computes along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens, and vertically through its layers. Attention has made the horizontal axis very wide. The vertical one between steps is a straw — at each decoding step the model does a full forward pass, produces a rich top-layer hidden state, samples one discrete token from it, and throws the rest away. Everything the model "thought" that didn't make it into that token is gone.
extra_html:
Wang, Cai, Langford and colleagues widen that channel. In their full-bandwidth transformer, the previous step's top-layer hidden state is fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed back in as the next input. Non-verbalized computation gets to re-enter the stack from the bottom with a renewed depth budget, and the architecture, KV cache, and plain language-modeling objective all stay standard. The catch is training: naive feedback destroys parallel teacher forcing, so they use a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining and mixes in a small fraction of deeper passes for stability.

Training 1B-parameter models up to 400B tokens, the authors report improvements in validation loss, 5-shot evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance — summarized as matching or approaching a standard transformer trained on roughly 1.5x more tokens, with negligible per-token decoding cost and shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy. These are the authors' results at 1B scale; whether the advantage holds at frontier scale is still open. Details and ablations in the paper.

related.title: Attention Is All You Need
related.hook: Drop recurrence and convolution, keep only attention — and you get a model that trains in parallel and powers nearly every LLM since.

related.title: Latent Context Language Models: Compressing the Prompt, Not the Cache
related.hook: Instead of shrinking the KV cache, compress the prompt itself: a small encoder folds a long context into a few latent embeddings that a bigger decoder reads — letting agents skim and expand on demand.

related.title: How Much Is Left? LLMs Linearly Encode Their Remaining Output Length
related.hook: Before an LLM writes a single token of its answer, its hidden state already seems to know roughly how long the answer will be — and the estimate jumps when it restarts a draft.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'narrow channel' the full-bandwidth transformer widens?

choices.text: The vertical feedback between decoding steps — only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack
The horizontal attention span, which limits how far back a token can look
The KV cache bandwidth between GPU memory and compute units

flashcards.explanation_html: Dense attention already gives broad horizontal access to the past. The bottleneck is vertical: the top-layer hidden state is thrown away at each step, and only the discrete sampled token survives.

flashcards.prompt: How is the previous hidden state reintroduced?
flashcards.back_html: It's fused with the sampled token embedding through a gated linear unit and fed in as the next step's input — so non-verbalized computation re-enters the stack with a renewed depth budget.

flashcards.prompt: Why does training need a scheduled multi-pass objective?
flashcards.back_html: Naive latent feedback breaks parallel teacher forcing. The authors introduce feedback late in pretraining and mix in a small fraction of deeper feedback passes, keeping training parallel and stable.

flashcards.prompt: What headline efficiency claim do the authors make for 1B models trained to 400B tokens?

choices.text: Matching or approaching a standard transformer trained on roughly 1.5x more tokens
A 14x reduction in total pretraining FLOPs
Equal quality with half the model parameters

flashcards.explanation_html: The claim is data efficiency at negligible per-token decoding overhead — plus shorter reasoning traces at equal or better accuracy.
